01 · Know the exam

Pattern before preparation

Use the paper structure to decide what deserves time. Prelims demands breadth and accuracy; Mains rewards recall, judgement and written expression.

150 questions

General Studies in objective format; 150 marks and 2 hours are indicated in current cycle summaries.

Negative marking

Current summaries report one-third deduction. Follow the exact OMR instructions, including the unattempted option, in your notice.

Screening only

Prelims scores select candidates for Mains; they do not usually enter the final merit total.

General Hindi

Qualifying paper. Do not neglect grammar, précis, comprehension and expression; a failure here can stop evaluation of merit papers.

Merit papers

General Studies I, General Studies II and Essay form the descriptive core in current summaries. Optional treatment has varied by cycle.

Write to score

Answers need structure, Bihar examples, relevant data and a balanced conclusion—not a dump of memorised notes.

Personality

Clarity, honesty, composure, administrative judgement and awareness matter more than theatrical confidence.

Bihar lens

Prepare your district, graduation subject, work profile, state challenges, development priorities and recent public issues.

DAF command

Every word you submit can become a question. Build short, evidence-based talking points around it.

Non-negotiable: read the official advertisement, corrigenda and admit-card instructions for your own cycle. Eligibility, reservations, qualifying papers and marking can differ.

06 · Mains answer craft

Make every page easy to reward

A strong answer is not the longest one. It identifies the demand, gives organised evidence and closes with an administratively useful way forward.

D
Decode the directiveDiscuss, analyse, evaluate, examine and comment require different depth.
S
Structure before sentencesTake 30–45 seconds: introduction, 3–5 subheads, conclusion.
E
Evidence + BiharAdd a constitutional provision, report, example, case or local administrative lens.
W
Way forwardEnd with feasible, balanced and rights-respecting recommendations.

Progressive answer-writing ladder

  1. Weeks 1–2: write only outlines for one PYQ a day.
  2. Weeks 3–4: write three full answers each week without strict timing.
  3. Weeks 5–8: write five timed answers weekly; self-check relevance and structure.
  4. After week 8: one sectional test weekly plus a full essay every fortnight.
  5. Final phase: full-length papers at the actual pace and word limits in your notice.
Self-check: answered the exact question · balanced dimensions · Bihar link · readable headings · sourced data with year · complete conclusion.

How to use this section: finish one tab at a time. Turn each bold term into a question, practise the fact table, and attach one Bihar example to every national concept. The official advertisement remains final for the exact paper scheme.

Bihar history: the connected timeline

Ancient core: Magadha’s fertile middle-Ganga plain, river routes, elephants and access to iron-bearing regions supported state formation. Rajagriha was an early capital; Pataliputra later became the imperial centre of the Nandas and Mauryas. Buddhism and Jainism both have deep Bihar connections: Bodh Gaya, Rajgir, Vaishali, Pawapuri and Nalanda form a linked religious-intellectual landscape.

Learning and empire: Nalanda flourished for centuries as a residential centre of Buddhist learning. Vikramshila, associated with the Pala ruler Dharmapala, became another major institution. The Mauryan legacy connects administration, Ashoka’s dhamma, roads and trade; the Pala age connects Bihar to Buddhist scholarship and art.

Medieval to colonial: Sher Shah Suri of Sasaram is remembered for administrative and road reforms. Patna grew as a river-trade centre. In 1857, Veer Kunwar Singh led resistance from Jagdishpur. Gandhi’s 1917 Champaran Satyagraha addressed the exploitation of indigo cultivators through inquiry, mobilisation and non-violent pressure.

Modern state: Bihar and Orissa became a separate province in 1912; Orissa separated in 1936. Dr Rajendra Prasad, India’s first President, was a major national leader from Bihar. The state of Jharkhand was carved out of southern Bihar in 2000.

Bihar geography: regions, rivers and hazards

Position: Bihar is landlocked. Nepal lies to the north, Jharkhand to the south, Uttar Pradesh to the west and West Bengal to the east. The Ganga flows west to east and divides the state into broad north and south plains.

North Bihar: Himalayan rivers—including the Kosi, Gandak, Burhi Gandak, Bagmati, Kamla-Balan and Mahananda—carry large sediment loads. Low gradient, intense monsoon flow, channel migration and drainage congestion combine to create floods.

South Bihar: rivers such as the Son, Punpun, Falgu and Kiul-Harohar descend from the peninsular edge or plateau region. Rainfall variability can create drought stress even while the north faces floods. The Kaimur plateau and hills in the south-west contrast with the alluvial plains.

Ecology: Valmiki Tiger Reserve lies in West Champaran. The Gangetic dolphin is a flagship river species. Wetlands moderate floods, recharge groundwater, support fisheries and host migratory birds; their degradation is therefore both an ecological and livelihood issue.

Bihar economy and society: the analytical map

Agriculture: paddy, wheat, maize, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables and horticulture matter. Bihar’s comparative strengths include litchi, makhana, banana and vegetables. Small holdings, irrigation quality, storage, processing, market access and climate risk determine farmer income more than crop output alone.

Employment: a large workforce remains tied to low-productivity agriculture and informal work. Migration can ease local unemployment and bring remittances, but it can also expose weak local job creation, skill mismatch and social-security portability gaps.

Development chain: education and health improve human capital; roads, power and digital access reduce transaction costs; law and order plus predictable regulation support investment; urban planning and industrial clusters create non-farm jobs. A strong answer links these rather than listing schemes.

Social lens: examine gender, caste, disability, rural–urban location and district variation without stereotypes. Use constitutional equality, capability expansion and last-mile access as the frame.

Bihar polity, administration and culture

Institutions: Bihar has a bicameral legislature—the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council. The Governor is the constitutional head; the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister exercises executive authority under the constitutional scheme. District administration links state departments with local implementation.

Local government: Panchayats and municipalities handle constitutionally assigned local functions, but outcomes depend on funds, functionaries, planning capacity, social inclusion and public accountability. Gram Sabha participation, social audit, grievance redress and transparent procurement improve legitimacy.

Culture: Maithili, Magahi, Bhojpuri, Angika and other languages reflect regional diversity. Madhubani/Mithila painting, Manjusha art, Tikuli art, Sujni embroidery, Sikki craft, Chhath, Sonepur Mela and the Buddhist–Jain–Sikh heritage circuit are recurring exam areas.

Ancient India: state, society and ideas

Harappan civilisation: urban planning, drainage, standardized weights, craft specialization and long-distance trade are central features. The script remains undeciphered, so claims about political structure or language require caution.

Vedic transition: later Vedic society saw territorial kingdoms, expanding agriculture and stronger varna differentiation. The mahajanapadas emerged by the sixth century BCE; Magadha’s location and resources aided its rise.

New religions: Buddhism taught the Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path; Jainism emphasized the three jewels and strict ahimsa. Both challenged ritual dominance and used accessible languages. Mauryan governance combined a large imperial apparatus with regionally varied control.

Gupta and post-Gupta: achievements in literature, mathematics, astronomy and art coexist with debates over land grants, social hierarchy and political decentralization. Avoid calling any age “golden” without naming for whom and in which fields.

Medieval India: power, economy and culture

The Delhi Sultanate used military-fiscal institutions such as the iqta; the Mughal mansabdari–jagirdari system linked rank, service and revenue assignment. Akbar expanded alliance-building and imperial integration. Agrarian production, inland trade, ports and crafts supported a complex economy.

Bhakti and Sufi traditions: diverse teachers stressed devotion, ethical life and spiritual experience in regional languages. They were not one uniform movement. Architecture developed through interaction among regional traditions, court patronage, new structural forms and local artisans.

Modern India: Company rule to independence

Colonial expansion: the East India Company moved from trade to territorial power after Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764). The Diwani grant of 1765 gave revenue rights in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Land-revenue systems reshaped agrarian relations; deindustrialization, commercialization and wealth transfer became major nationalist critiques.

1857: multiple causes included military grievances, annexation, dispossession and local discontent. It was widespread but not all-India; leadership and aims differed by region. In Bihar, Kunwar Singh was a principal leader.

National movement: moderate constitutional politics was followed by Swadeshi, Home Rule, Gandhian mass movements, revolutionary activity and negotiations. Champaran (1917), Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India broadened participation. Independence came with Partition and immense violence.

Art and culture: how to revise

Classify architecture by structure, patronage and purpose; sculpture by material, iconography and school; literature by language and period; music by tradition and form. Link stupas and rock-cut caves to Buddhism, temple styles to regional adaptation, and Indo-Islamic forms to arches, domes, calligraphy, gardens and local craft.

For Bihar, connect Mauryan polish and pillars, Bodh Gaya, Nalanda, Pala sculpture and manuscripts, Patna Kalam, Madhubani painting and regional folk traditions.

Earth, landforms and climate

Plate tectonics explains major mountain belts, earthquakes and volcanism. Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion removes it; deposition builds features. Rivers create V-shaped valleys upstream, meanders and floodplains on gentler slopes, and deltas where deposition exceeds removal.

Indian monsoon: differential heating, seasonal pressure change, movement of the ITCZ, cross-equatorial flow, jet streams, relief and ocean-atmosphere variability interact. The Himalaya blocks cold continental air and forces uplift; the Western Ghats create orographic rainfall and a rain shadow.

India: soils, agriculture, resources and population

Alluvial soils dominate the northern plains; black soils are moisture-retentive and linked to Deccan basalt; red and laterite soils occur across weathered peninsular regions. Soil fertility depends on texture, organic matter, nutrients, water and management—not colour alone.

Kharif crops are mainly sown with the monsoon; rabi crops in the cooler post-monsoon season; zaid crops occupy the short summer interval. Cropping choice follows water, soil, temperature, market and risk. Population geography examines density, distribution, migration, urbanisation and the demographic transition.

Environment and ecology

An ecosystem transfers energy through trophic levels while nutrients cycle. Food webs improve resilience; keystone species can have effects disproportionate to abundance. Biodiversity exists at genetic, species and ecosystem levels. In-situ conservation protects habitats; ex-situ conservation includes zoos, botanical gardens and seed banks.

Pollution: PM2.5 penetrates deep into lungs; eutrophication follows nutrient enrichment; biomagnification increases persistent contaminants up a food chain. Climate mitigation reduces emissions or increases sinks; adaptation reduces harm. Disaster-risk reduction combines hazard, exposure, vulnerability and capacity.

Bihar applied geography

Explain north Bihar floods through transboundary Himalayan catchments, intense rainfall, sediment, low slope, embankment effects and settlement in floodplains. Explain south Bihar drought stress through rainfall variability, groundwater and irrigation access. A complete answer adds forecasting, resilient housing, drainage, wetland restoration, crop planning and basin cooperation.

Map practice should include the Ganga, Son, Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati, Punpun and Mahananda; Valmiki Tiger Reserve; Kaimur plateau; Bodh Gaya, Rajgir, Nalanda, Vaishali, Vikramshila and major district headquarters.

Five environment distinctions

  • Weather is short-term atmospheric condition; climate is the long-term pattern.
  • Hazard is a potentially damaging event; disaster results when it meets exposure and vulnerability.
  • National park generally has stricter protection than a wildlife sanctuary; exact rights and boundaries follow law.
  • Mitigation addresses causes of climate change; adaptation addresses effects.
  • Renewable describes replenishment; it does not automatically mean zero ecological impact.
Constitutional foundation

The Preamble expresses justice, liberty, equality and fraternity and identifies India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic. Fundamental Rights are enforceable; Directive Principles guide the state but are not directly enforceable; Fundamental Duties are citizen obligations. Courts often seek harmony between rights and directive principles.

Basic structure: Parliament can amend the Constitution under Article 368, but cannot destroy its basic structure. Judicial review, constitutional supremacy, rule of law, federalism, secularism and free and fair elections are among principles recognised in case law.

Union and state institutions

The President and Governor are constitutional heads operating largely on ministerial advice, subject to limited constitutional discretion. The Prime Minister/Chief Minister leads the Council of Ministers, which is collectively responsible to the lower house. Parliament and state legislatures legislate, control finance and hold the executive accountable.

The Supreme Court and High Courts protect rights, review government action and interpret law. The Comptroller and Auditor General audits public expenditure; the Election Commission supervises elections; Finance Commissions recommend fiscal distribution.

Federalism and local government

Legislative subjects are distributed through Union, State and Concurrent Lists. Residuary power rests with Parliament. Federal practice also depends on fiscal transfers, intergovernmental consultation and institutions such as the GST Council and Inter-State Council.

The 73rd and 74th Amendments constitutionalised rural and urban local bodies. Effective decentralisation needs the “3Fs”: functions, funds and functionaries. In Bihar answers, add ward-level services, Gram Sabha participation, social audit and district planning.

Rights, accountability and governance

Article 14 protects equality before law and equal protection of laws; Article 19 guarantees specified freedoms subject to reasonable restrictions; Article 21 protects life and personal liberty. Articles 32 and 226 enable constitutional remedies. Reservations seek substantive equality under constitutional provisions.

Good governance rests on legality, transparency, participation, responsiveness, efficiency and accountability. RTI, legislative questions, audit, citizen charters, grievance systems and independent oversight reduce information and power asymmetry.

National income, growth and inflation

GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within domestic territory. GVA measures value added by producers; GDP at market prices equals GVA plus product taxes minus product subsidies. Nominal values use current prices; real values remove price change using a base year.

Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, not a one-time increase in one item. Demand-pull, cost-push and supply shocks differ in cause and policy response. CPI tracks retail prices; WPI mainly tracks wholesale goods. High inflation can erode purchasing power, while very low inflation may signal weak demand.

Money, banking and public finance

The RBI manages monetary policy, currency, banking regulation and financial stability. A higher repo rate generally raises borrowing costs and restrains demand, though transmission is neither immediate nor complete. CRR is the cash banks keep with RBI; SLR is the share of specified liquid assets they maintain.

Revenue receipts do not create liabilities; capital receipts include borrowings and recovery of loans. Revenue deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total non-borrowing receipts. Primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest payments.

Agriculture, industry and external sector

Agricultural productivity depends on seed, soil, water, extension, credit, mechanisation, storage and markets. MSP is an announced support price for specified crops; procurement is the actual purchase and is not identical to MSP coverage. Food processing can reduce waste and increase local value addition.

Industry needs infrastructure, skills, finance, reliable regulation and market access. The current account records trade in goods and services plus income and transfers; the capital/financial account records investment and other financial flows. Currency depreciation can support exports but raises the domestic cost of imports.

Bihar economy: answer-ready framework

Begin with structural features: agriculture’s employment role, limited formal industry, migration, urbanisation, infrastructure and human development. Then diagnose productivity and inclusion gaps. For solutions, combine irrigation efficiency, crop diversification, farmer organisations, cold chains, food processing, skill–industry links, MSME finance, women’s work participation and stronger towns.

Do not copy a current number without its year. For any Budget or Economic Survey figure write: indicator → year → comparison → implication. A figure earns marks only when it supports an argument.

Physics in everyday life

Newton’s laws connect force and motion; momentum is mass × velocity and is conserved in an isolated system. Work is force × displacement in the force direction; power is the rate of doing work. Pressure equals force per unit area, explaining sharp tools and hydraulic systems.

Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation. Sound needs a medium; light can travel through vacuum. A convex lens converges parallel rays and can form real or virtual images depending on object position; a concave lens diverges. Household electrical energy is measured in kilowatt-hours.

Chemistry and materials

Atoms form elements; compounds contain elements chemically combined in fixed proportions; mixtures retain component properties. Acids donate hydrogen ions in aqueous solution, bases provide hydroxide ions or accept protons, and neutralisation forms salt and water. pH below 7 is acidic, 7 neutral and above 7 basic at ordinary conditions.

Oxidation involves loss of electrons or addition of oxygen; reduction is the opposite partner process. Corrosion is an oxidation process. Polymers are large molecules made from repeating units. Biodegradable does not mean instantly harmless; conditions and by-products matter.

Biology, health and nutrition

The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. DNA carries hereditary information; genes are functional DNA segments. Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy. Respiration releases usable energy from food.

Vaccines train immune memory; antibiotics act against bacteria and do not cure viral infections. Balanced nutrition needs macronutrients and micronutrients. Public health combines clean water, sanitation, vaccination, surveillance, primary care, nutrition and behaviour change.

Technology and space

Artificial intelligence finds patterns or generates outputs from data; bias can enter through data, objectives and deployment. Machine learning does not equal human understanding. Encryption protects confidentiality; hashing is one-way integrity checking; digital signatures support authenticity and integrity.

Satellites in geostationary orbit appear fixed over the equator and suit communications/weather monitoring; polar and sun-synchronous orbits suit repeated Earth observation. Remote sensing records reflected or emitted energy and supports crops, floods, forests and urban planning.

High-yield science traps

  • Mass is amount of matter; weight is gravitational force.
  • Power and energy are not the same: power is energy per unit time.
  • Viruses are not treated with antibiotics.
  • Ozone is protective in the stratosphere but harmful as a ground-level pollutant.
  • A gene-edited organism need not contain DNA from another species.

Current-issues notebook · reviewed 26 September 2026: these are durable issue briefs rather than daily headlines. Update statistics from the newest official document, but keep the cause–impact–response structure.

Flood resilience in Bihar

Why: Himalayan catchments, concentrated monsoon rainfall, sediment load, low-gradient plains, channel migration, drainage obstruction and settlement exposure. Impacts: crop loss, displacement, disease, schooling interruption, damaged roads and repeated household debt. Response: forecasting, last-mile warning, floodplain zoning, resilient shelters and roads, wetland restoration, local disaster plans, transparent relief and transboundary basin coordination.

Migration, skills and job creation

Why: labour-force growth, small holdings, uneven industrialisation, wage differences and skill–job mismatch. Two-sided effect: remittances and mobility can raise household resilience, but unsafe work and family separation create costs. Response: portable social protection, credible skill certification, worker information centres, labour-intensive manufacturing, food processing, construction quality, MSME clusters and stronger intermediate towns.

Education and foundational learning

Enrolment alone does not prove learning. Diagnose teacher support, attendance, early-language instruction, classroom practice, assessment, nutrition, digital access and transition to secondary school. Priorities include foundational literacy and numeracy, regular low-stakes assessment, remedial teaching, teacher mentoring, safe schools and district-level public dashboards.

Public health and nutrition

Health outcomes reflect primary care, referral transport, workforce, medicines, water, sanitation, food diversity and women’s agency. A good policy answer connects prevention with treatment: vaccination and surveillance, functional health-and-wellness centres, maternal care, nutrition counselling, anaemia reduction, clean water and accountable supply chains.

Agriculture, climate and value addition

Farm risk combines weather, price, pests, water and small marketable surplus. Solutions should be crop- and district-specific: water management, climate-resilient seed, advisories, farmer-producer organisations, storage, grading, processing, contract safeguards, crop insurance reform and better links to urban markets.

Urbanisation, air and municipal capacity

Bihar’s growing towns need land-use planning, drainage, public transport, affordable housing, waste segregation, sewage treatment and clean construction. Air pollution comes from multiple seasonal sources, so enforcement must combine transport, road dust, waste burning, industry, household energy and regional coordination.

Digital governance with safeguards

Digital systems can reduce delay and leakage, but exclusion can arise from poor connectivity, authentication failure, language barriers or inaccessible design. Use assisted access, offline alternatives, minimal data collection, cybersecurity, appeal routes, audit trails and human review for high-stakes decisions.

Current-affairs answer formula

Issue → background → Bihar link → affected groups → constitutional/institutional frame → evidence with year → benefits and risks → feasible way forward. Separate fact from opinion and name the source of every dynamic number.

Mental ability essentials

Percentage

x% of y = xy/100. Successive changes a% and b% give net change a + b + ab/100, using negative signs for decreases.

Ratio and proportion

If a:b = m:n, write a = km and b = kn. Divide a total T in m:n as Tm/(m+n) and Tn/(m+n).

Average

Average = total/number. When one observation changes by d, the average changes by d/n.

Profit, loss and interest

Profit% = profit/cost price × 100. Simple interest = PRT/100. Compound amount = P(1 + r/100)n.

Time and work

If A finishes in x days, A’s one-day work is 1/x. Add work rates, not days. For pipes, treat an outlet as a negative rate.

Speed

Speed = distance/time. Average speed for equal distances at speeds a and b is 2ab/(a+b), not their simple average.

Data interpretation

Read title, unit, base year and axis before calculating. Percentage-point change and percentage change are different.

General Hindi essentials

शब्द-शुद्धि

वर्तनी, लिंग, वचन, कारक, संधि, समास, उपसर्ग–प्रत्यय, पर्यायवाची, विलोम और मुहावरों का नियमित अभ्यास करें। नियम के साथ उदाहरण लिखें।

वाक्य-शुद्धि

कर्ता–क्रिया का मेल, काल, सर्वनाम, परसर्ग और अनावश्यक पुनरुक्ति जाँचें। लंबे वाक्य को दो स्पष्ट वाक्यों में बाँटना प्रायः बेहतर होता है।

संक्षेपण

मूल भाव पहचानें, उदाहरण और पुनरावृत्ति हटाएँ, अपने शब्दों में लगभग एक-तिहाई आकार का सुव्यवस्थित अनुच्छेद लिखें और उपयुक्त शीर्षक दें।

बोध

उत्तर केवल गद्यांश से निकालें। लेखक का मुख्य तर्क, कारण, परिणाम और प्रयुक्त स्वर अलग-अलग पहचानें। निजी राय न जोड़ें जब तक प्रश्न न माँगे।

निबंध

भूमिका में विषय का अर्थ स्पष्ट करें; मुख्य भाग में सामाजिक, आर्थिक, प्रशासनिक, नैतिक और बिहार-विशिष्ट आयाम दें; निष्कर्ष संतुलित और समाधानमुखी रखें।

Explained practice set

Answer before opening. Each explanation teaches the elimination logic, not only the correct option.

1. Which factor most directly helped Magadha’s early expansion? A) Maritime isolation B) Fertile plains and resource access C) Desert cavalry D) European trade
Answer: B
The middle-Ganga plain supported agriculture and transport, while nearby iron-bearing regions and elephants strengthened state capacity. The other choices do not describe Magadha’s setting.
2. Vikramshila Mahavihara is chiefly associated with which dynasty? A) Pala B) Chola C) Kushana D) Lodi
Answer: A · Pala
Dharmapala of the Pala dynasty is associated with its foundation. It became a major centre of Buddhist learning.
3. What made Champaran Satyagraha distinctive? A) A naval mutiny B) Inquiry into indigo cultivators’ grievances C) Demand for separate electorates D) Protest against salt tax
Answer: B
The 1917 movement investigated the exploitative indigo system and used non-violent mobilisation. Salt belongs to the 1930 Civil Disobedience phase.
4. The Ganga’s broad role in Bihar is best described as: A) flowing north–south B) dividing broad north and south plains C) forming the Nepal border D) draining only the plateau
Answer: B
The Ganga runs broadly west to east through Bihar and separates the north and south plains.
5. Why are north Bihar rivers highly flood-prone? A) Tidal waves only B) Himalayan sediment, monsoon flow and low gradient C) No tributaries D) Permanent drought
Answer: B
Heavy sediment and high seasonal discharge meet a flat plain, encouraging deposition, drainage congestion and channel change.
6. Valmiki Tiger Reserve is in: A) West Champaran B) Gaya C) Bhagalpur D) Nalanda
Answer: A · West Champaran
It occupies Bihar’s north-western edge near the Nepal border and is the state’s tiger reserve.
7. Which pairing is correct? A) Article 32—Finance Commission B) Article 280—Finance Commission C) Article 324—CAG D) Article 368—Right to Equality
Answer: B
Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission. Article 32 concerns constitutional remedies, 324 the Election Commission and 368 amendment.
8. The “3Fs” of decentralisation are: A) food, fuel, finance B) functions, funds, functionaries C) federalism, freedom, franchise D) farms, factories, forests
Answer: B
Local bodies need assigned responsibilities, adequate finance and staff to turn constitutional status into real capacity.
9. Which body audits government expenditure? A) Election Commission B) CAG C) Finance Commission D) NITI Aayog
Answer: B · Comptroller and Auditor General
The CAG audits public accounts; the Finance Commission recommends fiscal distribution rather than auditing expenditure.
10. Fiscal deficit broadly equals: A) revenue expenditure only B) total expenditure minus non-borrowing receipts C) tax revenue minus grants D) exports minus imports
Answer: B
It measures the government’s overall financing gap and approximate borrowing requirement.
11. Real GDP differs from nominal GDP because it: A) excludes services B) removes price change using a base year C) counts imports only D) is always higher
Answer: B
Real GDP values output at constant prices to separate quantity growth from inflation.
12. An increase in repo rate generally aims to: A) reduce borrowing costs B) restrain inflationary demand C) abolish taxes D) increase rainfall
Answer: B
A higher policy rate tends to make credit costlier and moderate demand, though transmission varies.
13. Which process raises persistent pollutant concentration at higher trophic levels? A) Nitrogen fixation B) Biomagnification C) Transpiration D) Succession
Answer: B
Persistent contaminants accumulate in organisms and become more concentrated up a food chain.
14. Climate adaptation means: A) reducing vulnerability to effects B) only cutting emissions C) measuring weather once D) banning all development
Answer: A
Adaptation reduces harm from actual or expected effects; mitigation addresses causes by reducing emissions or increasing sinks.
15. Antibiotics are ineffective against: A) bacterial pneumonia B) viral infection C) some bacterial wounds D) bacterial tuberculosis
Answer: B · viral infection
Antibiotics target bacterial structures or processes. Misuse against viruses contributes to antimicrobial resistance.
16. A digital signature primarily supports: A) authenticity and integrity B) screen brightness C) file compression D) internet speed
Answer: A
It helps verify who signed and whether the signed data changed; it does not itself hide the content.
17. A finishes work in 12 days and B in 18 days. Together, one-day work is: A) 1/30 B) 5/36 C) 1/6 D) 30
Answer: B · 5/36
Add rates: 1/12 + 1/18 = 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36. Together they finish in 36/5 days.
18. A value rises 20% and then falls 20%. Net change is: A) zero B) 4% increase C) 4% decrease D) 20% decrease
Answer: C · 4% decrease
Take 100 → 120 → 96. Equal percentage changes use different bases.
19. In précis writing, the best first step is to: A) copy opening lines B) identify the central argument C) add personal examples D) retain every quotation
Answer: B
The précis must preserve the core meaning while removing examples, repetition and ornament.
20. Which is the strongest Mains conclusion on Bihar floods? A) “Nothing can be done” B) “Build only embankments” C) a basin, land-use, resilience and local-capacity package D) repeat the introduction
Answer: C
A multi-causal problem needs a coordinated response spanning river basin, floodplain, infrastructure, ecosystems and community preparedness.

Model Mains answer · Floods in Bihar

Demand: show why the problem is both physical and administrative, then propose workable reform.

  1. Introduction: North Bihar lies in low-gradient plains crossed by sediment-rich Himalayan rivers.
  2. Geographical causes: intense monsoon flow, sediment deposition, channel migration and drainage congestion.
  3. Governance causes: floodplain occupation, fragmented basin planning, maintenance gaps, vulnerable housing and weak last-mile warning.
  4. Consequences: crop loss, disease, schooling disruption, migration, damaged connectivity and repeated household debt.
  5. Way forward: basin cooperation, forecasting, floodplain zoning, wetland restoration, resilient infrastructure, crop adaptation, local drills and transparent relief.
  6. Conclusion: shift from seasonal relief to risk-informed development while preserving livelihoods and river ecology.
04 · Minimum effective library

One core source per subject

The goal is repeated revision, not collecting books. Search the list by topic, then use PYQs to decide depth.

12 sources
History foundation

NCERT History

Classes 6–12 selections; build chronology and concepts before advanced summaries.

Read → timeline → PYQs
Modern India

Spectrum / Bipan Chandra

Choose one modern-history text. Annotate Bihar’s role alongside every national phase.

One source only
Culture

NIOS / CCRT notes

Selective coverage of architecture, religions, art, literature, music and Bihar heritage.

Use with image recall
Geography

NCERT + G.C. Leong + atlas

Physical concepts first, then India and Bihar mapping. Practise blank maps every week.

Map while reading
Polity

M. Laxmikanth

Use as a framework, not scripture. Link articles and institutions to current cases and Bihar governance.

Revise in cycles
Economy

NCERT + one economy manual

Master concepts, then update with Union/Bihar Budget and Economic Survey documents.

Concept → current example
Science

NCERT science 6–10

Prioritise everyday applications, biology and environment; use a compact GK source only for revision.

Concept + MCQs
Environment

NCERT biology + concise manual

Ecology, biodiversity, pollution, laws, climate and Bihar’s protected areas/wetlands.

Static + current
Bihar special

One Bihar GK manual

Use it as an index, then verify fast-changing figures against official survey and budget sources.

Never memorise stale data
Current affairs

Newspaper + PIB + PRS

Record only issue, background, Bihar relevance, data, arguments and way forward.

45 minutes daily
Qualifying Hindi

Grammar + précis workbook

Practise weekly. A qualifying paper deserves insurance, not last-week panic.

One timed page/week
Exam intelligence

BPSC previous papers

Solve first, classify each question by topic, and let frequency shape your revision.

07 · PYQ method

Mine papers; do not merely solve them

Previous papers reveal the commission’s language, depth and recurring zones. Use a four-pass system.

Pass 1 · Diagnose

Attempt cold. Mark every answer as know / confused / guessed / unknown. Do not look at solutions mid-paper.

Pass 2 · Classify

Tag each question by syllabus topic, Bihar-specificity and source. Repeated tags become priority chapters.

Pass 3 · Repair

Write the reason your answer failed: concept gap, fact gap, poor elimination, haste or misreading.

Pass 4 · Re-test

Reattempt wrong questions after 7 days and the full paper after 30 days under timed conditions.

Study Plan

05 · 12-month roadmap

Build, practise, compress, perform

Start Mains answer writing before Prelims. Delay only the volume—not the habit.

Months 1–3

Foundation

  • Read syllabus + 5 PYQs
  • NCERT/core books
  • Begin Bihar notebook
  • 20 MCQs/day
Months 4–6

Integration

  • Finish first reading
  • 50 MCQs/day
  • 3 answers/week
  • Monthly current affairs
Months 7–9

Testing

  • Sectional tests
  • PYQ second pass
  • Essay every fortnight
  • Revise Bihar data
Months 10–12

Exam mode

  • Full timed mocks
  • Short-note revision
  • Error-log repair
  • Sleep and pace
01

Daily

Static subject + current affairs + MCQs/answer writing + recall without notes.

02

Weekly

One timed test, one Bihar issue brief, one map session and a full error-log review.

03

Monthly

One full revision cycle, one essay, backlog deletion and source-list pruning.

09 · Personality test

Prepare judgement, not a performance

Create a one-page dossier for each theme below. Speak in short, reasoned answers; acknowledge trade-offs and facts you do not know.

Your district

Economy, history, geography, administration, two problems and workable solutions.

Your profile

Graduation, employment gaps, hobbies, achievements and why public service now.

Bihar today

Development, education, health, floods, migration, agriculture, cities and social inclusion.

Why BPSC, and what would public service let you do that your current path would not?
Choose one persistent problem in your district. What can a subdivisional officer realistically change in one year?
How would you balance fast relief, due process and limited resources during a flood?
Name one Bihar policy you support and one improvement you would recommend.
What would you do if a lawful order is unpopular but necessary?
